title: Why Do I Get Hangovers So Easily? 7 Real Reasons (and What Helps)
excerpt: Get hungover after just a drink or two? How genes like ALDH2, congeners, sleep, body size, sex, age, and medications change how hard alcohol hits you, and what actually helps.
metaDescription: Why you get hangovers so easily: ALDH2 genes, congeners, sleep, body size, sex, age, and medications explained, plus why some people never get them.
author: DHM Guide Team
tags: why do i get hangovers so easily
content:
**The honest answer first:** if you get hangovers more easily than your friends, it's usually not in your head and it's usually not a single cause. The biggest pieces are your genes (especially how fast your body clears acetaldehyde, a toxic by-product of alcohol), how much alcohol actually reaches your blood per drink (body size, sex, food, and pace), what you drink (darker drinks carry more of the extra compounds called congeners), how badly alcohol wrecks your sleep, and whether you take any medicines that change how alcohol is handled. Age can play a part too, though not always the way people expect. Most people who feel "hangover-prone" have two or three of these stacked together.

**The quick checklist:** If you flush red, get a racing heart, or feel sick after a drink or two, read the genetics section and take it seriously. If you feel rough after just one drink, check your medicines and look at the "hangover after one drink" section below. If you mostly drink dark spirits or red wine, try clear drinks for a few weeks and compare. If you sleep badly after drinking, that alone can make the next day feel much worse. And whatever the cause, the only reliable fix is drinking less, more slowly, with food and water.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. **Talk to a doctor if** you react strongly to small amounts of alcohol, you have flushing with a fast heartbeat or trouble breathing, you get pain anywhere in your body after drinking, you take prescription medicines and aren't sure whether they mix with alcohol, or your hangovers are getting noticeably worse over time. Some prescription drugs (such as metronidazole and disulfiram) can cause a severe reaction with even small amounts of alcohol. In an emergency, call 911.

## What a Hangover Actually Is (So the Causes Make Sense)

A hangover is the set of symptoms you get after blood alcohol falls back toward zero: headache, tiredness, nausea, thirst, poor concentration, low mood, and sensitivity to light and sound. Researchers still don't fully agree on the mechanism, and that matters, because it means there isn't one single "hangover switch" that some people have and others don't.

The main contributors that researchers point to are:

- **Acetaldehyde.** Your liver turns alcohol into acetaldehyde, which is toxic, and then turns that into harmless acetate. If the second step is slow, acetaldehyde lingers.
- **Inflammation.** Heavy drinking triggers an immune response. Studies have found raised levels of inflammatory signaling molecules (cytokines) during hangovers, and some researchers think this explains a lot of the "flu-like" feeling.
- **Poor sleep.** Alcohol helps you fall asleep but disrupts the second half of the night.
- **Dehydration and stomach irritation.** Alcohol makes you urinate more and irritates the stomach lining, which contributes to thirst, headache, and nausea, though dehydration alone doesn't explain hangovers.
- **Congeners.** Extra compounds produced during fermentation and aging, found in larger amounts in darker drinks.
- **A rebound effect in the brain.** Alcohol calms the nervous system while it's in your blood; as it leaves, the brain is briefly over-excited, which shows up as jitteriness and anxiety.

The single biggest driver of how bad a hangover is remains simple: **how much you drank and how high your blood alcohol got**. Everything else in this article changes how strongly you react to a given amount. For the full picture of the underlying biology, see our [hangover science hub](/never-hungover/complete-hangover-science-hub-2025).

## Reason 1: Your Genes Change How You Process Alcohol

Genetics is the most important "it's not your fault" factor, and it's also the one people most often overlook.

### Twin studies say hangover sensitivity is partly inherited

A large twin study from Australia, published in the journal *Addiction* in 2014 (Slutske and colleagues), compared identical and fraternal twins and concluded that a meaningful share of the differences in how often people get hangovers is explained by genes, even after accounting for how much they drink. The exact share varied by sex and by how the question was asked, so it's best read as "genes matter a fair amount" rather than as a precise number. The practical point: if your parents or siblings also say they get wrecked by a few drinks, that's a real signal.

### ALDH2: the "flush" gene

The best-understood genetic effect involves an enzyme called **ALDH2** (aldehyde dehydrogenase 2). Its job is to clear acetaldehyde. A common variant, often written ALDH2*2, makes the enzyme much less effective. It's most common in people of East Asian descent, where estimates suggest it's carried by a large minority of the population.

People who carry one copy usually get the classic **alcohol flush**: a red face and neck, a warm feeling, a faster heartbeat, and sometimes nausea or a headache after a small amount of alcohol. People who carry two copies often feel so unwell after drinking that they avoid alcohol altogether.

Research on hangovers in this group is more mixed than you might expect. A study in the *Journal of Studies on Alcohol* in 2000 (Wall and colleagues) found that Asian American college students with one copy of the variant reported more hangover symptoms than those without it, at similar drinking levels. That fits the acetaldehyde theory. But because flushing is so unpleasant, many carriers also drink less, which complicates comparisons.

One important safety point: carriers of the ALDH2 variant who keep drinking regularly have a **substantially higher risk of esophageal cancer**, because acetaldehyde is a known carcinogen. Taking an antacid to hide the flush (a common trick) hides the warning sign but not the damage. Our [complete guide to Asian flush](/never-hungover/complete-guide-asian-flush-comprehensive) covers this in detail, including what you can and can't do about it.

### ADH1B and other genes

Another enzyme, **ADH1B**, handles the first step (turning alcohol into acetaldehyde). Some variants make that step faster, which can produce a quick burst of acetaldehyde. These variants are also more common in East Asian populations and are linked to lower rates of heavy drinking. Research on how ADH1B affects hangovers specifically is limited, so it's fair to say it probably contributes in some people but we don't have clean data on how much.

Beyond these well-known genes, hangover sensitivity is likely influenced by many small genetic differences, including ones related to inflammation and the brain's response to alcohol. Consumer genetic tests can tell you if you carry the ALDH2 variant, but they can't give you a reliable overall "hangover score." For what genetic testing can and can't tell you, see our [guide to alcohol metabolism and genetic testing](/never-hungover/alcohol-metabolism-genetic-testing-complete-personalized-health-guide-2025).

**What to do with this:** if you flush, take it as your body telling you that acetaldehyde is building up. Drinking less is the only real fix. No supplement reliably makes up for a weak ALDH2 enzyme.

## Reason 2: Congener Sensitivity (What You Drink, Not Just How Much)

Congeners are the extra compounds in alcoholic drinks besides ethanol and water: methanol, other alcohols, aldehydes, tannins, and flavor compounds. Fermentation and barrel-aging produce more of them, so darker drinks (bourbon, brandy, dark rum, red wine) generally have more than clear ones (vodka, gin, white rum).

The best-known study here was published in *Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research* in 2010 (Rohsenow and colleagues). Volunteers drank either bourbon or vodka to a fairly high blood alcohol level under controlled conditions. Hangovers were somewhat worse after bourbon than after vodka, although the difference was modest and the overall amount of alcohol still mattered most. In other words, switching drinks helps a bit, but it doesn't turn a heavy night into a light one.

Methanol is one of the congeners that gets the most attention. Your body breaks methanol down into formaldehyde and formic acid, but only once ethanol has mostly cleared, because both compete for the same enzyme. Some researchers think this delayed breakdown helps explain why hangovers peak when blood alcohol is near zero. It's a plausible idea, but not proven.

Some people also seem more sensitive to particular things found in certain drinks:

- **Red wine** contains histamine, tannins, and other compounds that some people react to with headaches. Sulfites get blamed a lot, but sulfite sensitivity mostly causes breathing problems in people with asthma rather than headaches, and white wine often has similar or higher sulfite levels.
- **Beer** contains gluten and yeast by-products that a small number of people react to.
- **Sweet mixed drinks** go down fast and hide how much alcohol you're having, which raises blood alcohol more than it feels like it should.

If you notice that one type of drink hits you much harder than another at the same amount, believe your experience. Try a few weeks of clear spirits with a simple mixer and see whether the pattern holds. Our guides to [whiskey hangovers](/never-hungover/whiskey-hangover-why-it-happens-prevention-guide), [vodka hangovers](/never-hungover/vodka-hangover-why-it-happens-prevention-guide), and [wine hangovers](/never-hungover/wine-hangover-guide) break down each type, and our explainer on [congeners in alcohol](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol) goes deeper on the chemistry.

## Reason 3: Alcohol Wrecks Your Sleep More Than You Realize

A lot of what feels like "a bad hangover" is really a bad night's sleep.

Alcohol is sedating at first, so you may fall asleep quickly. But as your body processes it during the night, sleep becomes lighter and more broken. REM sleep (the dreaming stage tied to memory and mood) tends to be suppressed early in the night, and you're more likely to wake up in the early morning hours and struggle to get back to sleep. Alcohol also relaxes the throat muscles, which makes snoring and sleep apnea worse in people prone to them.

Some people are simply more affected by this than others. If you already sleep lightly, have sleep apnea, or need a full eight hours to function, a night of drinking will hit you harder. Late nights add to the problem: a night out often means going to bed hours later than usual and getting up at your normal time.

Researchers have found that poor sleep after drinking is linked to worse hangover symptoms, and sleep loss on its own produces tiredness, headache, poor concentration, and irritability, which overlap heavily with a hangover.

**What to do with this:** stop drinking a few hours before bed so more of the alcohol is processed before you sleep, protect your sleep the night after, and if a partner says you snore heavily or stop breathing, mention it to a doctor. For the details, see our analysis of [alcohol and REM sleep](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-rem-sleep-complete-scientific-analysis-2025).

## Reason 4: Body Size and Sex Differences

The same number of drinks produces different blood alcohol levels in different people, and blood alcohol level is the strongest predictor of how bad a hangover will be.

### Body size and body water

Alcohol spreads through the water in your body. Someone with a smaller body, or with a lower proportion of body water, ends up with a higher alcohol concentration from the same drink. This is the main reason a smaller person will often feel worse after "only" matching a bigger friend drink for drink.

### Why women often feel it more per drink

Women, on average, reach a higher blood alcohol level than men after the same amount of alcohol. The main reasons are well established:

- **Less body water on average**, even at the same body weight, because of differences in body composition.
- **Smaller average body size.**
- **Possibly less alcohol broken down in the stomach** before it reaches the blood, though how big this effect is has been debated.

Hormones may also play a role. Some studies suggest alcohol is processed somewhat differently across the menstrual cycle and with hormonal contraception, but the findings are inconsistent, so it's hard to give practical rules beyond "notice your own patterns."

Here's the nuance worth knowing: when researchers have compared men and women at the **same blood alcohol level**, differences in hangover severity have generally been small. So the main sex difference isn't that women's bodies "do hangovers worse." It's that the same number of drinks produces more alcohol in the blood. Matching a partner or friend drink for drink is often the hidden cause. For more on sex-specific considerations with supplements and alcohol, see our guide to [DHM for women](/never-hungover/dhm-women-hormonal-considerations-safety-2025).

## Reason 5: Age (It's More Complicated Than "Hangovers Get Worse After 30")

Almost everyone over 30 says their hangovers got worse. The research is surprisingly mixed.

Large surveys have found that older adults actually **report fewer hangovers** than younger adults. A big Danish population survey, for example, found hangover frequency fell with age. Part of that is because older people tend to binge less often. But it means there's no strong evidence that aging itself makes every hangover worse.

That said, there are believable reasons why some people genuinely feel worse as they get older:

- **Less body water.** Muscle mass and body water tend to decline with age, so the same drink produces a higher blood alcohol level.
- **Slower recovery and worse sleep.** Sleep often gets lighter with age, and alcohol makes that worse.
- **More medicines.** Older adults are more likely to take medications that interact with alcohol (see the next section).
- **More responsibilities the next day.** In your twenties you could sleep until noon. Now you have work, kids, or early commitments, so you notice the hangover more.
- **Less frequent drinking.** If you drink less often than you used to, you may have lost some of the short-term tolerance you once had.

So if hangovers feel worse than they did at 22, you're probably right that something changed. It just may be your body composition, sleep, medicines, and schedule rather than "age" as such. Our guide for [adults over 50](/never-hungover/dhm-adults-over-50-age-related-safety-2025) covers age-related safety in more depth.

## Reason 6: Medications and Health Conditions

This is the section where "hangover-prone" can shade into "actually unsafe," so it's worth reading carefully.

### Medicines that can cause a severe reaction

Some prescription drugs block the same acetaldehyde-clearing enzyme that ALDH2 variants weaken, or otherwise cause a reaction that looks like a severe flush: flushing, pounding heart, nausea, vomiting, and headache. The best-known are:

- **Disulfiram (Antabuse)**, prescribed specifically to make drinking unpleasant.
- **Metronidazole and tinidazole**, antibiotics commonly prescribed for certain infections. Labels advise avoiding alcohol during treatment and for a period afterward.

These are prescription-only, and if you're taking one, follow your doctor's or pharmacist's instructions about alcohol exactly. Other drugs have been reported to cause milder versions of this reaction; your pharmacist can check your list.

### Medicines that make alcohol's effects stronger

Many common medicines add to alcohol's sedating effects or change how you feel the next day:

- **Sleep aids, anxiety medicines (such as benzodiazepines), opioid pain medicines, and some muscle relaxants.** Combining these with alcohol can dangerously slow breathing. This is a real safety risk, not just a worse hangover.
- **Antihistamines**, including many over-the-counter allergy and "nighttime" cold products. These add drowsiness and can leave you groggier the next day. Our guide to [DayQuil and alcohol](/never-hungover/dayquil-and-alcohol) covers cold medicines specifically.
- **Some antidepressants and other psychiatric medicines.** Effects vary a lot by drug. Ask your prescriber.
- **Diabetes medicines**, especially insulin and sulfonylureas, because alcohol can cause low blood sugar, which can feel like a hangover but is more dangerous.

### Painkillers taken for the hangover itself

Many people make the next morning worse by reaching for the wrong pain reliever. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) combined with regular heavy drinking is a known liver risk, and anti-inflammatory painkillers like ibuprofen and naproxen can irritate a stomach that alcohol has already irritated. See our guides to [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) and [Aleve and alcohol](/never-hungover/aleve-and-alcohol) before you take anything.

### Health conditions that can make you more sensitive

- **Migraine.** Alcohol, and red wine in particular, is a common migraine trigger. If your "hangover" after small amounts is a one-sided, throbbing headache with nausea or light sensitivity, it may be a migraine. Our guide to [alcohol headaches](/never-hungover/alcohol-headache-why-it-happens-how-to-prevent-2025) explains the difference.
- **Reflux and stomach conditions**, which alcohol aggravates.
- **Anxiety disorders**, which can make the post-drinking rebound ("hangxiety") much stronger. See our [hangxiety guide](/never-hungover/hangxiety-complete-guide-2026-supplements-research).
- **Liver disease**, which slows alcohol processing. If you have any liver condition, talk to your doctor about whether you should drink at all.

For a broader list, including how supplements like DHM fit in, see our [medication interactions safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025). If you're not sure about any medicine you take, a pharmacist can check it in a couple of minutes, and that's free.

## Reason 7: How You Drink on the Night

Two people can drink the same total amount and have very different mornings depending on how they drank it.

- **Drinking on an empty stomach.** Food in your stomach slows how fast alcohol reaches your bloodstream, which lowers your peak blood alcohol level. Drinking before dinner, or skipping dinner, is one of the most common reasons a "normal" night turns into a bad morning.
- **Drinking fast.** Shots, drinking games, and sweet drinks you finish quickly all push blood alcohol up faster than your liver can keep up with. Your liver clears roughly one standard drink an hour, and nothing speeds that up much.
- **Not drinking water.** Water won't cancel out alcohol, but alternating drinks with water slows your pace and helps with thirst and dry mouth.
- **Smoking.** People who smoke more while drinking tend to report worse hangovers. A study of college students in the *Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs* in 2013 (Jackson and colleagues) found that heavier smoking on drinking days was linked to worse hangovers, even after accounting for how much they drank.
- **Mixing with energy drinks.** Caffeine can mask how drunk you feel, which often leads people to drink more than they otherwise would.
- **Mixing drink types.** Despite the rhyme, the order you drink things in doesn't seem to matter much; a 2019 study in the *American Journal of Clinical Nutrition* found no difference between beer-then-wine and wine-then-beer. What matters is the total. More in our piece on the [beer before liquor myth](/never-hungover/beer-before-liquor-myth).

## Why Do I Get a Hangover After Just One Drink?

If one drink reliably leaves you feeling rough, it's worth thinking about this differently from an ordinary hangover, because a full hangover from a single standard drink is unusual. The most common explanations are:

1. **You carry an ALDH2 variant.** If you also flush, feel your heart race, or get nauseous quickly, this is the most likely cause. Acetaldehyde builds up even at low doses.
2. **A medicine is interacting with alcohol.** Check every prescription and over-the-counter product you take, including allergy pills and sleep aids.
3. **The drink is triggering a migraine or a reaction**, rather than a hangover. Red wine, histamine-rich drinks, and certain beers are common culprits for people prone to migraine or with histamine sensitivity.
4. **The "one drink" was bigger than you think.** A large pour of wine, a strong craft beer, or a cocktail with several shots can easily be two or three standard drinks. In the US, a standard drink is about 14 grams of alcohol: 12 oz of 5% beer, 5 oz of 12% wine, or 1.5 oz of 40% spirits.
5. **Something else made you feel bad.** Poor sleep, not eating, a late night, dehydration from heat or exercise, or coming down with a cold can all make one drink feel like many.
6. **You rarely drink.** People who drink very occasionally often notice the effects of a small amount more than regular drinkers do.

**When to see a doctor:** a strong reaction to very small amounts of alcohol, especially with flushing, hives, wheezing, a racing heart, or swelling, deserves a medical check. True alcohol allergy is rare, but alcohol intolerance and reactions to ingredients in drinks are not. In rare cases, pain after drinking alcohol (for example in the chest or in swollen lymph nodes) can be a sign of an underlying condition, so it's worth mentioning to a doctor rather than putting it down to a hangover.

## Why Do Some People Never Get Hangovers?

Almost everyone knows someone who claims they never get hangovers. Some of them are telling the truth, but it's less common than it sounds.

Researchers who study hangovers have looked at this directly. In surveys of drinkers, a minority report never having hangovers. But when researchers look at how much those people actually drank, many of them simply never got their blood alcohol very high. Among people who regularly drink to high levels, true "hangover resistance" appears to be uncommon. Studies of university students in the Netherlands and Canada, led by researchers in the Alcohol Hangover Research Group, have found this pattern: the higher the estimated blood alcohol, the smaller the share of people who said they avoided a hangover.

The reasons some people get away with it probably include:

- **Genetics.** The same twin research that shows some people are more prone also implies that others are naturally less prone.
- **Body size.** Bigger people reach a lower blood alcohol from the same drinks.
- **Drinking habits they don't notice.** Eating well, drinking slowly, drinking water, and stopping earlier than they think.
- **Better sleep after drinking.**
- **Different reporting.** Some people feel tired and foggy but don't call it a hangover.

There's also a less comforting possibility. Feeling fine after heavy drinking is not a sign that alcohol isn't harming you. A low response to alcohol (needing more to feel its effects) has been linked in long-term research to a higher risk of developing alcohol problems later. Not getting hangovers doesn't protect your liver, heart, or brain from the effects of heavy drinking. A hangover is uncomfortable, but it's also feedback.

## Why Some Hangovers Last Two Days

If your hangovers stretch into a second day, the same factors in this article usually explain it: a very high blood alcohol level, a badly disrupted night (or two) of sleep, a lot of dark spirits or wine, not eating, and less resilience as you get older. Accumulated sleep debt is a big one: if you were short on sleep before the night out, the hangover often lingers. Our guide to the [two-day hangover](/never-hungover/two-day-hangover) covers why it happens and what helps. If you regularly feel unwell for two days or more after drinking, that's a good reason to look honestly at how much you're drinking and to check in with a doctor.

## What Actually Helps If You're Hangover-Prone

You can't change your genes, your age, or your sex, but you can change the things that stack on top of them.

### The things with the strongest evidence

1. **Drink less.** This is the only approach that reliably reduces hangovers for everyone. Setting a limit before you go out works better than deciding on the night.
2. **Slow down.** One drink an hour, with water in between, keeps your peak blood alcohol lower.
3. **Eat before and while drinking.** A proper meal lowers your peak blood alcohol.
4. **Choose lower-congener drinks.** Clear spirits with a simple mixer, or lighter beers and wines, are a modest improvement over dark spirits and heavy red wine. See our ranking of the [least hangover-prone alcohol](/never-hungover/least-hangover-alcohol-ranked).
5. **Protect your sleep.** Stop drinking a few hours before bed and give yourself time to sleep it off.
6. **Count your drinks honestly.** Big pours and strong beers add up fast.
7. **Check your medicines.** A two-minute conversation with a pharmacist can prevent a bad reaction.

For a complete, evidence-led plan, see our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover), and for the morning after, our [science-based hangover cure guide](/never-hungover/how-to-cure-a-hangover-complete-science-guide).

### Where DHM fits, honestly

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree. Animal research suggests it may support alcohol metabolism and reduce some of alcohol's effects on the brain, and there's growing interest in it for hangovers. But human evidence is still limited: there are few well-controlled human trials, and they're small. It is not a replacement for drinking less, it doesn't fix an ALDH2 variant, and it doesn't make it safe to mix alcohol with any of the medicines above.

If you want to try it, treat it as a small extra on top of the basics, not the plan itself. Our [honest review of the DHM evidence](/never-hungover/does-dhm-work-honest-science-review-2025) explains what the research does and doesn't show, the [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how people use it, and our [product reviews](/reviews) compare the options we've tested. If you just want a simple single-ingredient option, [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) is the lower-cost one we usually point people to. If you take prescription medicines, check with your doctor or pharmacist before adding any supplement.

## When "Hangover-Prone" Is a Signal Worth Listening To

Sometimes being easily hungover is just how you're built. Sometimes it's a sign that something needs attention. Talk to a doctor if:

- You flush, get a racing heart, or feel sick after very small amounts of alcohol.
- You get hives, wheezing, swelling, or trouble breathing after drinking.
- Your hangovers have suddenly become much worse without a change in how much you drink.
- You get pain anywhere in your body after drinking.
- You take prescription medicines and haven't checked whether they mix with alcohol.
- You notice you're drinking to feel better the next morning, or you find it hard to cut back.

If you're worried about your drinking, in the US you can call the free, confidential SAMHSA National Helpline at **1-800-662-4357**, available 24 hours a day.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why do I get hangovers so easily?**

Usually because several factors stack up: genes that make you clear acetaldehyde more slowly, a smaller body or lower body water that raises your blood alcohol per drink, drinking darker or higher-congener drinks, poor sleep after drinking, and sometimes medicines that interact with alcohol. How you drink on the night matters too, especially drinking on an empty stomach or drinking fast.

**Why do I get a hangover after only one or two drinks?**

The most common reasons are an ALDH2 gene variant (often with facial flushing), a medicine that interacts with alcohol, a migraine or reaction to something in the drink, or a drink that contained more alcohol than you thought. Poor sleep, not eating, or rarely drinking can also make small amounts hit harder. If you react strongly to small amounts, especially with flushing, a racing heart, or breathing problems, see a doctor.

**Why do some people never get hangovers?**

Some people are genetically less prone, are bigger, or drink in ways that keep their blood alcohol lower without realizing it. Research suggests true hangover resistance is uncommon among people who regularly drink to high levels. Not getting hangovers doesn't mean alcohol isn't causing harm, and a low response to alcohol has been linked to a higher risk of drinking problems later.

**Are hangovers genetic?**

Partly. Twin research suggests that a meaningful share of the differences in how often people get hangovers is explained by genes. The clearest example is the ALDH2 variant common in people of East Asian descent, which slows the clearance of acetaldehyde and causes alcohol flush. Many other genes probably contribute in small ways.

**Do women get worse hangovers than men?**

Women usually reach a higher blood alcohol level from the same number of drinks because of smaller average body size and less body water. At the same blood alcohol level, research has generally found only small differences in hangover severity. The practical takeaway is not to match a larger person drink for drink.

**Do hangovers get worse with age?**

Many people feel they do, but large surveys have found older adults report fewer hangovers, partly because they drink less heavily. Lower body water, lighter sleep, more medicines, and busier mornings can make hangovers feel worse for some older adults even if aging itself isn't the direct cause.

**Can medication make hangovers worse?**

Yes. Some prescription drugs, such as metronidazole and disulfiram, can cause a severe reaction with alcohol. Sleep aids, anxiety medicines, opioids, and antihistamines add to alcohol's sedating effects and can be dangerous in combination. Diabetes medicines can cause low blood sugar with alcohol. Ask a pharmacist to check anything you take regularly.

**Does the type of alcohol affect how easily I get hungover?**

Somewhat. Darker drinks like bourbon, brandy, and red wine contain more congeners, and a controlled study found bourbon produced somewhat worse hangovers than vodka at the same alcohol level. The difference is modest, though. The total amount of alcohol matters far more than the type.

**Will DHM stop me getting hangovers?**

No supplement reliably prevents hangovers. DHM has promising animal research and limited human data. It may be worth trying as an extra, but it won't override genetics, high blood alcohol, or medication interactions. Drinking less, more slowly, with food, is still the most effective approach.

faq.question: Will DHM stop me getting hangovers?
faq.answer: No supplement reliably prevents hangovers. DHM has promising animal research and limited human data. It may be worth trying as an extra, but it won't override genetics, high blood alcohol, or medication interactions. Drinking less, more slowly, with food, is still the most effective approach.
